arguments.heading: Argument session of April 29, 2026
paragraphs: This was the only argument session in the approved record. It was not a reargument. Three lawyers appeared: John Sauer for the government, Ahilan Arulanantham for the Syria challengers, and Geoffrey Pipoly for the Haiti challengers.

The government asked the Court to read the review bar broadly. It argued the bar covers the final TPS decision and every earlier step, including procedural ones. It said letting procedural challenges through would gut the bar, since substantive challenges can be relabeled as procedural. It also invoked Trump v. Hawaii as setting a forgiving standard for the constitutional claim.

The challengers asked the Court to read the bar narrowly. They said determination, read in context, refers to country-conditions assessments. They relied on McNary, Reno v. Catholic Social Services, and Bowen to separate final decisions from antecedent procedures. Their claim targets only whether the Secretary actually consulted and gathered country-conditions information.

The justices tested several assumptions. Justice Alito tested whether determination needs a non-ordinary meaning for the challengers to prevail. Chief Justice Roberts tested whether Trump v. Hawaii truly extends to these TPS terminations affecting people here now. Justice Barrett tested why Congress would allow procedural review while barring substantive review, and what standard would apply if consultation is reviewable.

Justice Sotomayor tested the consultation record. She asked whether brief emails were the extent of consultation for Syria and Haiti, and noted the Haiti inquiry sought State's views on country conditions. Justice Kavanaugh tested Congress's reasons for a broad bar and whether Syria's regime change counts as a significant conditions change. Justice Thomas tested what remains reviewable despite the jurisdiction-stripping provision.

Justice Jackson tested the statute's purpose, asking whether its thrust is humanitarian safety during armed conflict, and invoked Bowen's distinction between determinations and methods. Justice Kagan tested whether foreign-policy wording meaningfully distinguishes adequate consultation. Justice Alito warned that adequacy review of consultation could invite constant procedural challenges.

The government's answers conceded ground in places. It admitted the record shows only the cited emails for consultation. It agreed a no-procedure social media termination would not be reviewable. It said the review bar does not reach constitutional claims. It also agreed the terminations rested on national interests regardless of country conditions.

The challengers' answers narrowed their own claim. Arulanantham said the claim requires consultation about country conditions, not review of how meaningful the consultation was. He said challenges to the substantive safety of Syria are barred. He noted national interest is not a factor under the armed conflict basis. Pipoly adopted the Syria challengers' reading of the review bar for the Haiti the opposing sides.

No reargument session appears in the approved record, so nothing here reflects a later reargument changing or revisiting any point. The approved record does not support any additional sides, arguments, or facts beyond those described above.

case.dek: A plain-language guide to the Supreme Court argument on April 29, 2026

dek_sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case is about temporary protected status, a program the government calls TPS. It lets people from countries hit by war or disaster stay in the United States for a set period. The fight here is over the Secretary of Homeland Security ending that protection for Syria and Haiti.

The people who challenged the terminations wanted a court to check how the government made its decision. The government says a federal law blocks courts from reviewing these decisions at all. That kind of legal block is called a review bar. It means judges cannot second-guess the decision, even if they think it was a bad one.

So the big question is simple. Can judges look at how the Secretary handled required steps, like consulting other parts of the government, before ending TPS? Or does the law make all of that off-limits to courts?

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 5, lines 23-17

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Secretary ended TPS for Syria and Haiti. People who hold that protection, along with others, went to court to challenge those terminations. Lower courts handled the dispute before it reached the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court heard oral argument on April 29, 2026, starting at 10:35 in the morning. Three lawyers argued that day. John Sauer argued for the government. Ahilan Arulanantham argued for the Syria challengers. Geoffrey Pipoly argued for the Haiti challengers.
Oral argument is where justices ask questions and lawyers answer. Nothing said there decides the case. The justices vote and explain their decision later.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The government asks the Court to hold that the review bar covers everything. It says the law blocks courts from reviewing the final TPS decision and every earlier step, including procedural ones like consultation. It also asks the Court to treat the constitutional challenge under a very forgiving standard from an earlier case, Trump v. Hawaii.

The challengers ask the Court to read the review bar more narrowly. They say the law only blocks review of the government's judgments about conditions in each country. They want courts to still check whether the Secretary actually followed required procedures, like consulting the State Department about conditions on the ground.

The Haiti challengers adopted the same reading of the review bar as the Syria challengers. Both groups of challengers therefore asked for the same basic result: procedural compliance stays reviewable, while the substantive safety judgments stay off-limits.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government's lawyers made several points. They said the review bar covers any determination about TPS designation, extension, or termination. They argued that letting procedural exceptions through would gut the bar, because any substantive challenge could be relabeled as procedural. They also said TPS is meant to be temporary, and court orders would undermine that purpose.

The government's lawyers also made concessions. They admitted the administrative record shows only brief email exchanges for consultation, with nothing else identified. They agreed a Secretary could end TPS by social media post with no procedure and that would still not be reviewable. They also said the review bar does not reach constitutional claims.

The challengers' lawyers took a narrower path. They said their claim targets only whether the Secretary actually consulted and gathered information about country conditions. They said challenges to the substantive safety judgments themselves are barred. They leaned on older cases, including McNary, Reno v. Catholic Social Services, and Bowen, which separate final decisions from the steps taken before them.

The challengers also clarified what national interest means here. They noted national interest is not a factor under the armed conflict basis for TPS. That matters because the government's own lawyer agreed the terminations rested on national interests regardless of country conditions.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: The justices pressed both sides hard. Justice Alito asked whether the word determination needs an unusual meaning for the challengers to win. He also warned that letting courts review how thorough consultation was could invite endless procedural lawsuits.

Chief Justice Roberts asked whether the government's reliance on Trump v. Hawaii stretches that case to cover these TPS terminations. Justice Kavanaugh asked the government to explain why Congress would want such a broad review bar. He also asked whether regime change in Syria counts as a significant change in conditions.

Justice Sotomayor pushed hardest on the record. She asked whether brief emails were all the consultation that happened for Syria and Haiti. She noted the Haiti inquiry asked the State Department for its views on country conditions. She also posed a hypothetical about a Secretary ending TPS by social media with no procedure at all.

Justice Sotomayor also cited harsh public statements about other countries to probe whether discriminatory purpose mattered. Justice Jackson asked about similar statements and whether the statute's core purpose is humanitarian safety during armed conflict. Justice Barrett asked what review standard would apply if consultation is reviewable, and why Congress would allow procedural review while barring substantive review.

Justice Thomas asked what, if anything, remains reviewable despite the jurisdiction-stripping provision. That term means a law that removes courts' power to hear certain claims. Justice Kagan asked whether wording like foreign policy concerns meaningfully separates adequate consultation from inadequate consultation.

sections.heading: How the lawyers answered
paragraphs: The government's lawyer answered the hypotheticals directly. He agreed a social media termination with no procedure would not be reviewable. He said alleged failures to follow statutory steps are not reviewable either. He also said the statutory procedural steps, like consultation, would not be subject to court review.

On consultation itself, the government's lawyer said asking is enough. He argued that seeking input counts as consultation, and even no response or an unresponsive reply would still satisfy it. He said not asking would not be consultation, but maintained that any such failure still could not be reviewed by courts.

On the harsh statements, the government's lawyer said that, in context, they referred to crime and poverty rather than race. He did not concede that any deference standard would change the outcome, saying the same statements are before the Court either way. He also said the government must consider country conditions, but argued any failure to do so is not reviewable under the statute.

The challengers' lawyer answered the standard question by narrowing his claim. He said he seeks review only of whether the Secretary actually consulted and obtained country-conditions information, not of how meaningful or thorough that consultation was. He confirmed that challenges to the substantive safety judgments are barred under his own reading.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case tests how far Congress can go in shielding a government decision from judges. If the review bar covers everything, a Secretary could end TPS for any reason, or no reason, and no court could check it. That is what the government's own answers in argument suggested.

If the bar is narrower, courts could still enforce procedural promises Congress wrote into the law, like consulting the State Department. The challengers say that is the only thing left to review, since the substantive safety judgments stay off-limits either way.

The ruling will also shape how courts handle similar review bars in immigration law. Older cases like Bowen separate final decisions from the steps before them, and both sides claimed those cases support their reading.

sections.heading: What happens next
paragraphs: Nothing in oral argument decides the case. The justices will meet privately and vote. The Court will issue its decision in a later opinion, at a date it chooses.
Until then, the lower courts' handling of the terminations remains what it was. The Supreme Court's eventual ruling will set the final word on what the review bar covers.
